Subject: Performance SLOs + context window questions

Marissa / Dylan,

Thanks again for the call this morning — helpful overview. A few follow-ups from our infra and product teams as we scope the pilot:

- Context window: we need to pass up to ~60k tokens of historical context in a single request (document-level history + recent session). Generated output is usually ~800–1200 tokens.
- Latency SLO: target p95 end-to-end "response available" (first generated token streamed) <= 800ms for typical requests. For heavier requests (full 60k context + 1k output) we can accept up to 1.5s p95 as long as it's predictable.
- Throughput / concurrency: expected steady-state 50–100 qps, with bursts to 200 qps during peak business hours. Concurrent active sessions expected ~20k users but typical concurrency on the model endpoints will be 8–12 parallel requests.
- Streaming: required. Our product needs first-token streaming start within the SLO and then continued token streaming at low latency (we care about inter-token tail latency).
- Other: we will likely be on Dedicated or Private deployment; data residency in US required.

Can you confirm feasibility and provide rough perf numbers for an 80B-class model and a 13B-class model (baseline + optimized/quantized) for the two operating points: 8k context / 512 output and 60k context / 1k output? Also any guidance on batching/concurrency tradeoffs and whether KV caching helps with repeated prefixes.

I've attached our SLO questionnaire and two example session payloads. Happy to share more if you need representative inputs. Can we get a short write-up and suggested next steps?

Thanks,
Alex

Also any guidance on batching/concurrency tradeoffs and whether KV caching helps with repeated prefixes.

Alex — appreciate the clear SLO doc and sample payloads (attached). Short recap of where we stand and immediate next steps:

1) Feasibility: yes — Redwood Dedicated / Private can support 64k-ish context windows. There are tradeoffs: latency increases with context length (memory traversal + KV cache warmups) and batching increases throughput at the cost of tail latency.

2) Baseline numbers (high level, ballpark):
   - 13B model (optimized Q4/INT8 on latest kernels):
     * 8k context / 512 output: p95 first-token ~120–220ms, full 512-token stream completion p95 ~350–450ms (depends on output sampling rate).
     * 60k context / 1k output: p95 first-token ~450–700ms, full completion p95 ~1.1–1.6s.
   - 80B model (FP16 or GF32 kernels):
     * 8k / 512: p95 first-token ~240–420ms, completion p95 ~700–900ms.
     * 60k / 1k: p95 first-token ~900ms–1.4s, completion p95 ~1.8–2.6s (higher variance).

3) Streaming / first-token latency: streaming helps perceived latency since first-token can be emitted before full decode. For long contexts the dominant cost is the attention/KV warmup — we can often start streaming within the p95 numbers above for the first token. Inter-token latency is influenced by sampling/decoding speed; optimized kernels and integer quantization reduce inter-token tail.

4) Batching vs latency: automatic batching increases throughput but will add queueing latency at low QPS if you tune batch sizes aggressively. For your SLOs we recommend configuring a small max batch delay (e.g., 4–8ms) and per-route concurrency limits so steady-state latency doesn't exceed targets.

5) KV cache and repeated prefixes: KV caching helps a lot when requests share large prefixes. If your product can pin or re-use context (session-level caching) you'll see substantial latency reductions on repeat requests. For entirely unique 60k contexts, caching is less helpful.

6) Next steps we recommend:
   - Share representative sample payloads (you attached two; thank you). Please add a few heavier edge cases (largest docs).
   - We spin up a dedicated perf harness (we can do this in hosted sandbox or your Dedicated cluster) and run: steady-state 50/100 qps with concurrency knobs, and burst tests to 200 qps.
   - We'll produce a small matrix of p50/p95 p99 numbers for 13B vs 80B (baseline + quantized) for the two context sizes.

Dylan (cc) will call out technical recommendations for kernel/runtime knobs and expected test artifacts. We'll aim to share an initial perf report within 3 business days after we receive the full set of sample payloads.

Proposed meeting: 30 minutes next week to review results — are you available Wed 7/7 or Thu 7/8?

Thanks,

Marissa / Alex — quick technical note to supplement Marissa's recap.

On the metrics you asked for, here are practical considerations and knobs we'll exercise during the perf run: 

- Model variants: for 60k context we recommend testing both a dense 80B FP16 variant and a quantized 13B (INT8) variant. The 13B quantized model often offers the best cost/latency tradeoff for retrieval-heavy use cases.

- Memory / kernel behavior: large context lengths move memory access from on-chip cache to GPU memory and cause more KV memory traversals. We use sharded KV layouts and attention tiling to reduce overhead but there is unavoidable per-request startup for very long contexts.

- Streaming specifics: initial token emission pipeline:
   1) Tokenization + context pack (CPU) — typically 5–30ms depending on document size.
   2) KV assembly and attention priming (GPU) — dominated by context length; expect 150–400ms delta going from 8k to 60k on 80B models.
   3) First-token decode (GPU) — 20–100ms depending on model size and quantization.

- Inter-token latency: depends on decoder throughput; integer kernels and optimized sampling reduce per-token decode time. For 13B-INT8 we often see 4–8ms per token; for 80B-FP16 it's more like 8–15ms/token.

- Batching config: we'll run tests with two modes: low-latency (max batch delay 4 ms, small max batch size) and high-throughput (batch delay 20 ms). That will give you an operating curve to pick SLO vs cost.

- Concurrency and autoscaling: on Dedicated we recommend configuring reserved GPU slots to handle your steady concurrency (8–12) and autoscaling buffers for bursts. We'll simulate realistic arrival patterns (Poisson + bursts) in the harness.

- Observability: we'll attach token-level latency traces and per-route breakdown (tokenization, KV, decode) so you can see where tail latency originates.

Deliverables from the perf run: p50/p95/p99 for first-token and overall completion, inter-token latency distribution, GPU utilization, and recommended config for batch delay + concurrency.

If you can confirm the final sample set (especially the 5 largest examples) by EOD Friday 7/1 we'll start the run Monday and share results by Thu 7/7.

—Dylan
